planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed at the base of a tall pole or sturdy trellis, since the vigorous vines can reach 8-10 feet and will swamp light supports.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, training vines up a tall pole, corn stalk, or trellis rather than a light fence. Mostoller Wild Goose is a Pennsylvania heirloom pole bean with a famous origin story: seed was reportedly found in the crop of a wild goose shot in the 1860s and has been passed down through the Mostoller family ever since. The plump, kidney-shaped white beans with a faint pink blush cook to a smooth, creamy texture that many gardeners favor for baking and hearty winter soups. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, and expect strong vigor and heavy yields from a relatively small planting.
sources: Slow Food USA - Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; pick young for a flat snap bean or leave pods to fully dry on the bush for a mahogany-red dry shell bean.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained garden soil after frost danger has passed; the compact bush habit needs no staking, making it an easy dry bean for smaller gardens. Low's Champion is a New England bush bean introduced in 1884 by the Aaron Low Seed Company of Boston and believed to derive from an older Abenaki variety, producing broad, flat pods that can be picked young as tender snap beans or left to mature into glossy mahogany-red oval dry beans. Its dual usefulness as both a green bean and a soup bean made it a dependable staple in old New England kitchen gardens. Harvest pods regularly if using fresh to keep plants productive, or let the whole crop dry down at season's end for winter storage beans.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; this short, early-maturing bush bean suits short-season gardens and can also be fall-sown in mild climates.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the danger of frost; the low, compact bushes need no support and mature quickly compared with most dry beans. China Yellow, also called the Sulphur Bean, is a New England heirloom documented before 1870, valued for its small, plump, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that cook down quickly to a soft, creamy consistency ideal for stewing and baking. Despite the name, it has no connection to China; the name simply describes its distinctive pale yellow color. Let pods dry fully on the plant, then thresh and store the beans in an airtight container.

planting.note: Direct sow at the base of a trellis or pole after last frost; pick at about 3 inches, when the outline of the beans just bulges the pod, for the best snap-bean stage.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep and provide a tall pole or trellis, since this vigorous climber produces over a long season. Aunt Ada's Italian is a family heirloom pole bean brought from Italy to Colorado around the turn of the twentieth century, prized for its dual usefulness: the flat, tender pods make excellent snap beans when picked young, while pods left to mature and dry yield a flavorful soup bean. Its productivity and reliability across a long harvest window made it a treasured keeper variety passed down within one family for generations before wider seed-saver distribution. Pick regularly for fresh eating to keep vines producing, or let the last flush dry fully on the vine for winter storage beans.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile soil; this bush type needs no staking but has a longer season than most dry beans, so give it the full growing window.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained soil after frost danger passes; the sturdy bush plants carry four-inch pods that need no support. Marrowfat, also known as the White Egg bean for the plump, egg-shaped form of its seed, is a mid-1800s New England baking bean recognized by Slow Food USA's Ark of Taste for its creamy texture and rich, almost bacon-like savoriness when cooked. It was once a mainstay of the region's baked-bean tradition before falling out of common cultivation, and is now kept alive mainly by small seed savers and heirloom specialists. Allow pods to dry completely on the plant before shelling, and store the beans in a cool, airtight container for baking and soups through winter.
sources: Slow Food USA - Ark of Taste
